content: The document titled Recommendations and Guidance on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in July 2021. It provides detailed insights into the values and preferences of individuals regarding hepatitis C virus (HCV) self-testing (HCVST). The publication is available under a Creative Commons license, allowing non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo or any suggestion of endorsement by WHO is prohibited. The report was developed collaboratively by the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND), consultant Guillermo Z. Martínez-Pérez, and WHO, with support from Unitaid and the Government of the Netherlands. It is based on a multi-country rapid qualitative assessment conducted in 10 countries, including Brazil, Costa Rica, India, Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, the Philippines, Rwanda, South Africa, Thailand, and Ukraine. The assessment aimed to explore the acceptability and feasibility of HCVST among key populations and to inform the development of global normative guidance. Background Globally, over 70 million people are infected with HCV, yet the majority remain undiagnosed. Achieving global HCV elimination goals requires improved access to testing, which can increase awareness of HCV status and facilitate linkage to treatment. HCVST is an innovative approach that can expand testing access, particularly for populations not reached by traditional testing methods. Key populations at higher risk of HCV include people who inject drugs (PWID), people who use drugs (PWUD), men who have sex with men (MSM), people living with HIV (PLHIV), sex workers, and mobile or migrant populations. These groups often face barriers to accessing HCV prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services. Methods The assessment involved individual interviews, focus group discussions, and participatory action research (PAR) activities. It was conducted between July and November 2020, guided by a standardized master protocol. Depending on local COVID-19 restrictions, activities were conducted either face-to-face or via telephone/web-based platforms. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. Participants included individuals at increased risk of HCV, members of the general population, and healthcare workers (HCWs). Data collection included socio-demographic information and thematic analysis of participant responses. Results The assessment included 920 participants, of whom 66% were at increased risk of HCV, 16% were from the general population, and 18% were HCWs. Participants recognized HCVST as an innovative tool that could increase awareness of HCV status and motivate users to seek further care. They appreciated the privacy and confidentiality offered by self-testing. However, concerns were raised about potential errors if instructions were unclear and the risk of psychosocial harm. Participants emphasized the need for confirmatory testing following a reactive HCVST result. Participants suggested that HCVST service delivery models should be tailored to local contexts and accompanied by information on HCV prevention, treatment, and care. Many preferred that HCVST kits be provided free of charge, especially for underserved groups, and that instructions include illustrations and links to video tutorials. They also stressed the importance of avoiding stigma toward already marginalized populations. Conclusions HCVST is perceived as a valuable tool to increase HCV testing. Careful consideration must be given to addressing barriers and inequalities in access to HCV care, particularly for key populations. Ethical Considerations The assessment adhered to national norms and regulations for research and data protection. Participants provided written or verbal consent and were informed of the study's goals, potential risks, and their rights to withdraw or decline to answer questions. This report highlights the potential of HCVST to address gaps in HCV testing and care, particularly for underserved and high-risk populations. It underscores the importance of tailoring service delivery models to local needs and ensuring equitable access to testing and treatment.
